chapter.name: Understanding Social Science
chapter.blurb: What Social Science is, its four disciplines and their sources and methods, India's knowledge traditions, and why Social Science matters.

scope_in.item: Meaning of Social Science and its role in everyday life
Society through time; India's knowledge traditions (Panchamahabhutas, vasudhaiva kutumbakam, Arthashastra); how social scientists gather evidence
The core disciplines and Geography with its tools and holistic approach
History and its sources: literary, archaeological, epigraphic and numismatic; modern historiography
Political Science and Economics: governance, power, Indian political thought, economic decisions and India's economic history
Why we study Social Science; the future of Social Science; the Grade 9-10 learning journey

scope_out.item: Detailed chronology of Indian or world history
scope_out.reason: Only introduced later in the book

scope_out.item: Physical geography processes such as plate tectonics and climate
Detailed working of democratic institutions and elections
Economic theory such as demand and supply
Sociology, Philosophy, Anthropology and Psychology in depth
scope_out.reason: Named only; developed in higher grades

concepts.name: What Social Science is and how it shows up in daily life
concepts.description: Social Science as the systematic study of human society and the systems, such as governance, economy and environment, that shape everyday life.
concepts.idea: Social Science studies society and explains why events occur, how people live together and how different aspects of life connect.
concepts.rule: Social Science is the systematic study of human society. It explains why, not only what: society is shaped by history, geography, institutions, resources and human choices.
concepts.example: The food you eat, the road you travel and the electricity you use all depend on governance, economic production, social cooperation and the environment.

questions.a: Our food is harvested, transported and sold by many people, roads are planned by public authorities, schools follow educational policies and electricity comes through a vast network. Even simple activities rely on governance, economic production, social cooperation and the natural environment.

questions.a: Why do some regions depend on farming while others focus on industry or trade?
o: Why do some regions depend on farming while others focus on industry or trade?

questions.q: Give two questions from everyday observation that Social Science helps us answer.
questions.a: For example: Why do some people live in crowded cities while others live in scattered villages? Why do communities speak different languages and follow different traditions?

questions.q: A drought affects crops and farmers' incomes. Name two other aspects of society it also affects.
questions.a: It also affects government relief measures (politics), migration to cities (society) and traditional ways of coping with scarcity (culture).
s: One correct additional aspect such as politics or migration

questions.q: Write how a drought affects five aspects of society: environment, economy, politics, society and culture.
questions.a: Environment: crops are affected. Economy: farmers' incomes fall. Politics: governments make relief decisions. Society: people migrate to cities. Culture: traditional ways of coping with scarcity are used.
s: Culture effect and clear link to drought

questions.q: Why can no single field of study fully explain human society?
questions.a: Society is complex and has many connected aspects
o: Society is complex and has many connected aspects

Because society never changes over time or place
Because there is only one cause behind everything that happens

questions.q: Why does the chapter say Social Science shows society as "one connected story"?
questions.a: Simple observations show that people, places and systems are linked: economy, environment, government and culture all affect one another, so society is not a collection of separate pieces.
s: Says aspects of society are connected
Refers to people, places and systems linked together

questions.q: Observe a change in your locality over the past five years (transport, housing, education, technology or environment). Say what it was earlier, what changed, a cause and its effect on people.
questions.a: For example a new bus service: earlier people walked long distances; now travel is easier; the cause is the local authority starting the service; the effect is easier access to schools and markets.
s: Describes the earlier situation and the change
Describes the effect on people's lives

questions.q: Ravi says Social Science is only about memorising dates, maps and definitions. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. The chapter says Social Science is not about memorising; it is about understanding people, places, society, culture and power using observation, evidence and reasoning.
s: Says it is about understanding using evidence and reasoning

questions.q: Write three questions a social scientist might ask about a flood in a village: one about geography, one about the economy and one about government.
questions.a: Geography: Why is this region prone to floods? Economy: How did the flood affect farmers' incomes? Government: What relief did the government provide?

concepts.name: Society through time and India's knowledge traditions
concepts.description: How societies changed over time, the Indian ideas of Panchamahabhutas, vasudhaiva kutumbakam and the Arthashastra, and how social scientists work with evidence.
concepts.idea: India has a long tradition of understanding society through observation, discussion and reasoning, and social scientists still gather evidence from many sources.
concepts.rule: Panchamahabhutas: earth, water, fire, air, space. Vasudhaiva kutumbakam: the world is one family. Arthashastra (Kautilya, about 2,300 years ago): administration, economy, taxation, duties of rulers. Social scientists use observation, interviews, surveys, documents and comparison.
concepts.example: Villages grew into towns and towns into cities as people learnt farming, tool-making and trade.

questions.a: It says the world is one family, so human societies across regions and cultures are interconnected. Social Science studies such global interactions and relationships.

questions.a: They learnt to grow crops, domesticate animals, build settlements, develop tools, exchange goods and organise governance. Villages grew into towns and towns into cities.
s: Names two developments such as farming or tools

questions.q: Name two methods that social scientists use to gather evidence.
questions.a: They observe people's lives, conduct interviews and surveys, examine documents and compare different times and places.

questions.q: Explain how the Arthashastra shows that systematic thinking about governance is very old.
questions.a: The Arthashastra, attributed to Kautilya, was composed about 2,300 years ago. It examined administration, economic management, taxation and the duties of rulers, so such thinking existed long before modern academic disciplines.

questions.q: Explain how the chapter shows that the past shapes the present and today's actions shape the future.
questions.a: Societies evolved from early communities depending on nature to villages, towns and cities with institutions and new ideas. To understand the present we trace this journey of continuity and change, and today's decisions will influence the future.
s: Says the past shapes the present

questions.q: Meera says Social Science began only with modern universities. Evaluate.
questions.a: She is wrong. India's thinkers valued questioning and reasoning long ago, and works like the Arthashastra show systematic thinking about society long before modern academic disciplines.
s: Gives an ancient example such as the Arthashastra

concepts.name: The disciplines of Social Science and Geography
concepts.description: The four core disciplines of Grades 9-10 and the discipline of Geography, its tools and its holistic approach.
concepts.idea: Social Science draws on Geography, History, Political Science and Economics, each asking different questions about society.
concepts.rule: Geography studies the Earth, its environments and how people and places affect one another; it uses maps, globes, atlases, GIS and infographics and combines spatial and temporal perspectives. History studies the past; Political Science studies governance; Economics studies production, distribution and use of resources.
concepts.example: India's long coastline made it a hub of contact with Africa, Europe and Southeast Asia, a question Geography helps answer.

questions.q: Describe the four core disciplines of Social Science in one line each.

questions.q: Sam says Geography is only about memorising capitals and rivers. Evaluate.

concepts.name: History and the sources of history
concepts.description: How history studies the human past, the itihasa-purana tradition, modern historiography and the literary, archaeological, epigraphic and numismatic sources.
concepts.idea: Historians use many kinds of sources, from written texts to coins and inscriptions, to understand the past.
concepts.rule: Archaeological sources are material remains (monuments, sites, artefacts, art). Literary sources include texts, travelogues and memoirs. Epigraphic sources are inscriptions on durable materials. Numismatic sources are coins and currency. Modern historiography uses empirical evidence with tools such as carbon-14 dating and human genetics.
concepts.example: A coin of Samudragupta is a numismatic source; a Gupta-period Brahmi pillar inscription is epigraphic.

questions.q: Compare the itihasa-purana tradition with modern historiography.

questions.q: Why do historians use many different kinds of sources?

s: Says each type gives different evidence

concepts.name: Political Science and Economics
concepts.description: Political Science as the study of governance and power, Indian political thought, and Economics as the study of choices about limited resources.
concepts.idea: Political Science studies how power is shared and used; Economics studies how limited resources are used to meet needs.
concepts.rule: Political Science: constitutions, governments, institutions, power, social movements. Indian thought linked politics to dharma, artha and rajadharma and saw power as a responsibility. Economics: how goods and services are produced, exchanged and distributed, and decisions of consumers, producers and governments.
concepts.example: Panchayati Raj gives village citizens a voice in local development planning.

questions.q: What happened to India's economy under colonial rule?
questions.a: Colonial rule disrupted earlier progress and caused widespread poverty, recurrent famines and the decline of traditional industries.

questions.q: The text says economics is not only about numbers and markets. Explain what else it is about.
questions.a: It is also about well-being, equity and justice. It studies how decisions by consumers, producers and governments affect everyday life, jobs and services, and how to balance growth and fairness.

questions.q: Describe India's economic history as given in the chapter, including the challenges that remain.
questions.a: For centuries India was among the world's leading economies with trade, industry and maritime activity. Colonial rule brought poverty, famines and the decline of industries. After independence India rebuilt the economy and made progress, but challenges remain in raising incomes and ensuring growth reaches all sections.
s: Effect of colonial rule and later progress

questions.q: Ali says economics is only about money and markets. Evaluate.

concepts.name: Why we study Social Science and its future
concepts.description: The value of Social Science for understanding diversity, taking part in a democracy and facing future challenges.
concepts.idea: Social Science helps us understand systems around us, respect diversity, take part responsibly as citizens and connect the past, present and future.
concepts.rule: Differences in language, customs and occupations arise from geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors. Informed citizens ask questions about causes, effects and solutions. Social Science will help with climate change, sustainable development, social harmony and equitable use of resources.
concepts.example: Learning how governments make decisions prepares you to participate responsibly in civic life.

questions.q: Social Science connects
questions.a: the past, the present and the future
o: the past, the present and the future
only numbers and the sums that are done with them
only the future, without any reference to earlier times
only machines and the way that they are built

questions.q: Understanding differences in customs and languages builds
questions.a: respect and cooperation among communities
o: respect and cooperation among communities
conflict between communities, as differences increase
ignorance of other people's ways of life and beliefs
isolation, as communities keep away from one another

questions.q: In a democratic society citizens play an ____ role in public life.
questions.a: active

questions.q: Which of these will Social Science help societies address in the future?
questions.a: climate change and sustainable development
o: climate change and sustainable development
only sports rules and the way that games are played
only cooking methods and the recipes of a region
only entertainment, such as films and music of the day

questions.q: Differences in language and customs within one country are outcomes of
questions.a: geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors
o: geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors
chance alone, without any reason behind the differences
only one historical event, long ago in the past
weather only, which changes from one place to another

questions.q: The habit of careful questioning is essential because it helps to
questions.a: address problems that affect society as a whole
o: address problems that affect society as a whole
avoid all problems in society before they begin
stop discussion so that people agree without asking why
make decisions without evidence, quickly and confidently

questions.q: Indian culture binds diversity together through
questions.a: an underlying unity
o: an underlying unity
complete uniformity
ignoring differences
strict separation

questions.q: Understanding how governments function and decisions are made prepares you to
questions.a: participate responsibly in civic life
o: participate responsibly in civic life
avoid voting and leave all the decisions to others
stay unaware of laws that affect daily life
ignore rights and duties as a citizen of the country

questions.q: How does knowing about past decisions help us make wiser choices for the future?
questions.a: By understanding how past decisions shaped the present, we can see their results and learn from them, which helps us choose better for the future.
s: Says past decisions shaped the present
Says this helps in making wiser choices

questions.q: Which skills does the chapter say you have begun practising?
questions.a: careful observation, asking questions, examining evidence and recognising connections
o: careful observation, asking questions, examining evidence and recognising connections
only memorising dates, names and definitions from the book
only copying answers written by other students in the class
only drawing maps and diagrams from the textbook

questions.q: The skills include careful observation, asking questions, examining ____ and recognising connections.
questions.a: evidence

questions.q: The chapter says Social Science will guide the
questions.a: responsible use of new technologies
o: responsible use of new technologies
ban on all technology, so that society does not change
end of all change, so that customs stay as they are
removal of cities, so that people return to villages

questions.q: Give two reasons for studying Social Science.
questions.a: It helps us understand the systems around us, respect diversity, take part responsibly as citizens and ask informed questions about issues such as environment or employment.

questions.q: How does Social Science help us understand diversity within our country?
questions.a: It explains that differences in languages, customs and occupations arise from geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors, which builds respect and cooperation among communities.
s: Says differences arise from such factors
Says this builds respect and cooperation

questions.q: Choose one issue (environmental protection, public health, employment or urban growth) and show how you would ask informed questions about it.
questions.a: For urban growth: What are the causes (migration, jobs)? What effects does it have (traffic, housing, pollution)? What solutions could the government and citizens try?
s: Names an issue and its causes

questions.q: The purpose of Social Science stated at the end of the chapter is to prepare you to
questions.a: understand the world and take part in shaping it as informed and thoughtful citizens
o: understand the world and take part in shaping it as informed and thoughtful citizens
memorise a list of dates, names and events of the past
avoid public life and keep to oneself in one's home
leave your traditions behind and copy those of other places

questions.q: Why do differences like language and customs continue over time within the same country?
questions.a: They are outcomes of geographical, historical, cultural and economic factors that persist and are passed on, though Indian culture also binds them into an underlying unity.
s: Refers to the factors behind the differences

questions.q: The chapter calls the study of Social Science a journey. Describe the three stages of this journey.
questions.a: From understanding how societies evolved, to analysing how they function today, to imagining how they can become better in the future.

questions.q: Vik says Social Science is of no use in daily life. Evaluate.
questions.a: He is wrong. It explains the systems we depend on such as roads, markets and schools, helps us take part in civic life and think about problems like environment, health and employment.
s: Gives an example of everyday use

questions.q: Write a short paragraph on what being a responsible citizen means, using ideas from this chapter.
questions.a: A responsible citizen understands how government and society work, respects diversity, asks careful questions using evidence, takes part in civic life and thinks about the future.
s: Refers to understanding how government and society work
Refers to respect for diversity or questioning with evidence
Refers to taking part and thinking about the future
